notes:
I was able to read pages from Enduring Word, Bible Hub, StudyLight, Precept Austin, NET Bible, GotQuestions, Bible.org, Ligonier, The Gospel Coalition, Blue Letter Bible and New Advent. My search tool hit its usage limit before I got to the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), the Methodist and Holiness sites, the Pentecostal sites (ag.org, pneumareview.com, samstorms.org), oca.org or catholic.com. Some long pages were also cut short, so some commentators' notes on vv. 8–11 are missing. Anything I couldn't find is left out.

# Revelation 4: Research Notes

**v. 1: "A door standing open… Come up here"**

*Traditional reading*
- **The voice:** Most say it is the same trumpet-like voice as in 1:10, the voice of Christ. Ellicott says it's strange anyone has argued otherwise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/4.htm
  - Ligonier says the same. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/johns-vision-of-heaven
  - So does The Gospel Coalition's commentary. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/revelation/
- **Ellicott on the door:** John didn't see a door slowly opening; it was already open. Unlike visions where the sky splits apart (Ezekiel, Jesus' baptism), a door implies that the way into God's presence is open to faith (Heb. 10:19–20). He reads the whole chapter as comfort for a persecuted church: God rules over everything before the scenes of conflict begin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/4.htm
- **Ligonier:** Like Isaiah, John is commissioned as a prophet in heaven itself. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/johns-vision-of-heaven
- **Gill:** "Heaven" here is figurative, meaning the gospel church. Chapters 4–5 introduce the prophecy of the sealed book, just as chapter 1 introduced the seven letters. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/4-1.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Nothing justifies placing what follows in a time "after this world." "After these things" doesn't need to mean that. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/4.htm

*Where Protestant interpreters differ: is this a picture of the rapture?*
- **Yes, as a symbol (pre-tribulation view).** Guzik notes that many see it this way. A trumpet-like voice calls John up, as the church will be called up in 1 Thess. 4:16–17, after the churches are dealt with (chs. 2–3) and before God's wrath (ch. 6). He adds that the word "church" doesn't appear again until ch. 19. He also argues against reading chs. 4–19 as already fulfilled in the fall of Jerusalem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-4/
- **Bible Hub's Q&A page:** Argues the same way. "Church" appears 19 times in chs. 1–3 and then disappears until 22:16. It briefly argues against the mid-, post-tribulation and amillennial views. https://biblehub.com/q/Link_Revelation_4_1_to_rapture_concept.htm
- **Precept Austin:** Collects writers on both sides. It quotes some who say the verse can't prove a rapture and R. L. Thomas, who points out that John's body stayed on Patmos. The page's own view is that the passage is at least a "type" of the rapture. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-4-commentary
- **No.** Constable, though he writes about future events, says this is an invitation for John to enter heaven in his vision, not the church's rapture. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-4.html
- **Bible.org article:** Says the passage simply describes John receiving his vision. It notes that "after these things" appears several times in Revelation (7:1, 7:9, 15:5, 18:1) and marks a change of scene, not a change of era. https://bible.org/article/apocalypse-john-and-rapture-church-reevaluation
- **Coffman:**
  - The rapture is bodily, but John goes up "in the Spirit," so the verse can't refer to it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/revelation-4.html
  - He also cites Wilbur M. Smith: the text says nothing about a rapture, so it's questionable even to discuss one here. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/4-2.html

*Other views:* The NET Bible translates the Greek "with me" as "to me," because John only listens; it isn't a two-way conversation. It also notes that "like a trumpet" points back to 1:10. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rev&chapter=4

---

**v. 2: "In the Spirit… a throne… someone seated on it"**

- **Guzik:** The throne isn't empty. This rules out both atheism (no throne) and humanism (putting man on it). He quotes G. Campbell Morgan: at the centre of everything is an occupied throne. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-4/
- **Gill:** The one seated is God the Father, as distinct from the Lamb (5:6), but not excluding the Son and the Spirit. He rejects readings that make the three gemstones stand for the Trinity or for Christ's two natures. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/revelation-4.html
- **The Gospel Coalition:** The throne is the centre of the vision, and everything else is described in relation to it. Being "in the Spirit" (as in 1:10) confirms John as a true prophet. The commentary also shows that this throne becomes the throne of God and the Lamb in the new creation (22:1–3). https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/revelation/
- **NET Bible note:** "Spirit" could mean the Holy Spirit or John's own spirit. Either way, quoting Mounce, John was in a trance-like state of spiritual exaltation. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rev&chapter=4
- **Coffman:** The Greek doesn't mean a throne was being set up; it simply stood there. God's throne isn't a movable headquarters. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/revelation-4.html

---

**v. 3: Jasper, carnelian, emerald rainbow**

- **No physical description of God.**
  - Guzik, quoting Adam Clarke: John describes glory and brightness, not God's shape. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-4/
  - Barclay, quoting Swete: John avoids describing God in human form and pictures him in terms of light. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/revelation-4.html
  - D. A. Carson: You couldn't draw what John describes, and that may be the point. He compares Ezekiel 1, where the figure is only "like" a man. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/revelation-4-en/
- **The stones.**
  - Ligonier: Clear stones that light shines through, a picture of the brilliance of God's glory. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/johns-vision-of-heaven
  - Carson: The carnelian is a scarlet-red gem. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/revelation-4-en/
- **The rainbow.**
  - Ellicott: It recalls the covenant with Noah. It represents God's mercy wrapped around his judgment and his faithfulness in dark times. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/4.htm
  - Guzik: A throne means God can do whatever he wants; the rainbow means he binds himself to his promises. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-4/
  - Gill: The rainbow stands for the covenant of grace, always fresh like the green emerald. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/revelation-4.html
  - The Expositor's Bible: The rainbow points to grace, but mercy doesn't cancel God's justice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/revelation/4.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary suggests a green halo and tentatively links each stone to a meaning: purity, humanity and God's goodness in nature. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/4.htm
- **A caution:** Precept Austin questions R. L. Thomas's view that the green stands for grace. Since this is the only use of the Greek word for emerald in the Bible, it advises admitting we don't know rather than speculating. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-4-commentary

---

**v. 4: The twenty-four elders**

*Traditional reading: they represent God's redeemed people*
- **Ellicott:** The same word, "throne," is used for their seats and for God's (the KJV has "seats"), and 5:10 calls them kings and priests. They represent the whole church, Jewish and Gentile, from past and future. The 24 may be the twelve tribes plus the twelve apostles, or may echo David's 24 priestly divisions (1 Chr. 24). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/4.htm
- **Guzik:** Admits commentators are divided, but concludes the elders represent God's people. They sit on thrones because believers will reign with Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-4/
- **Ligonier:** Probably the twelve heads of the tribes and the twelve apostles (compare 21:12–14), standing for God's people throughout history. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/johns-vision-of-heaven
- **Barnes:** They are kingly, symbolic and human. "Elders" means venerable older men, not church officers. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/revelation-4.html
- **Gill** (StudyLight lists him as Baptist and Calvinist):
  - They are not the 24 books of the Old Testament, as some early writers held, and not angels, because 5:9 says they were redeemed.
  - He also rejects patriarchs plus apostles. Instead they are all members of the gospel church, numbered after the 24 priestly divisions.
  - Their white clothing is Christ's righteousness, and their crowns mean they reign over sin now and will reign with Christ for the thousand years.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/revelation-4.html
- **Matthew Henry:** The elders represent the Christian people. He applies the scene in a lesser sense to the church gathered for worship on earth, and in a fuller sense to the church in heaven. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rev/Rev_004.cfm

*Where interpreters differ: humans, angels, or the raptured church?*
- **The raptured church.** GotQuestions argues:
  - The Greek word for "elder" is never used of angels, who don't age.
  - White clothing usually belongs to believers.
  - Angels are never promised crowns. The word used is the victor's crown.
  - In ch. 5 the elders hold the prayers of the saints.
  - It rejects "Israel" and "tribulation saints" because neither had yet been redeemed at the time of the vision.
  - https://www.gotquestions.org/24-elders.html
- **Bible Hub (Arend Remmers' book overview):** The elders are believers already in heavenly glory after the rapture. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/por/tew/revelation.html
- **Angels, more likely.** The Gospel Coalition's commentary allows that they may represent all believers but thinks they most likely depict an order of exalted angels. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/revelation/
  - Carson points out that Paul calls some ranks of angels "thrones," and places the elders among the circles of heavenly beings. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/revelation-4-en/
- **Undecided.** Constable says they are either 24 human leaders (12 from Israel, 12 from the church) or 24 angels representing them. Everything John says fits angels, though "elder" is never used of angels elsewhere. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-4.html
- **Coffman's list of views:** He catalogues the main identifications: raptured church, Babylonian star gods, Jewish leaders (the Targum), priestly divisions, a special angelic order and others. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/revelation-4.html

*Other views*
- **Victorinus (early church, on New Advent):** The elders are the 24 books of the Law and the Prophets, and also the 12 patriarchs and 12 apostles. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0712.htm
- **NET Bible:** Points to its earlier note on "crown" at 3:11. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rev&chapter=4

---

**v. 5: Lightning, thunder; seven torches = seven Spirits**

- **Sinai.**
  - Ellicott: Signs of God's power to judge (Ex. 19:16; Ps. 97:2), rather than signs that judgment is about to fall. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/4.htm
  - Guzik: Like Sinai, they convey awe. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-4/
  - Ligonier: Like Sinai, they reassure God's people that he is in full control. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/johns-vision-of-heaven
  - Pulpit: Like Sinai, they symbolise God's power and majesty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/4-5.htm
- **Thunder as judgment.**
  - The Expositor's Bible: Lightning and thunder are always signs of judgment in Revelation, and the "torches" give a fierce rather than gentle light. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/revelation/4.htm
  - The Gospel Coalition: The same phrase returns at the climax of the seals, trumpets and bowls (8:5; 11:19; 16:18). https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/revelation/
- **Ellicott on the fire:** The fire is the Holy Spirit's purifying fire. He also suggests a link to the torch that passed between the pieces in God's covenant with Abraham (Gen. 15). So the rainbow (Noah), the torches (Abraham) and the thunder (Sinai) are all covenant signs. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/4.htm
- **Gill:** "Voices" are the gospel teachings. The seven lamps echo the tabernacle lampstand and stand for the Spirit's gifts in their fullness, giving light to the churches through preaching. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/4-5.html

*Where interpreters differ: who are the "seven Spirits"?*
- **NET Bible note:** Some take them as angels. Others take them as the sevenfold ministry of the Holy Spirit. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rev&chapter=4
- **The Holy Spirit:** Most of the sources I read take this view.
  - Ellicott: The Spirit in his many powers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/4.htm
  - Precept Austin's outline links it to Isaiah 11:2. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-4-commentary
  - The Gospel Coalition: The sevenfold Spirit. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/revelation/
- **Victorinus (early church):** The torches mean the gift of the Spirit, given through Christ's passion. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0712.htm

---

**v. 6: Sea of glass; four living creatures full of eyes**

*The sea*
- **Ellicott:** The world's throne sits on stormy "waters" of peoples (17:15). God's sea is calm, which pictures his counsels: deep but never murky. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/4.htm
- **Guzik:** Commentators disagree on whether it is real glass or only looks like glass. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-4/
- **Constable:** It may echo the temple washbasin, called a "sea" (1 Kgs 7:23). It would then picture the cleansing needed to approach God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-4.html
- **Barclay:** It suggests dazzling purity and the vast distance between John and the throne. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/revelation-4.html
- **NET Bible note:** The Greek word could mean rock crystal or ice. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rev&chapter=4

*The creatures*
- **Cherubim.** Guzik reads them as cherubim, based on Ezekiel 1 and 10. Their eyes show insight, not mindless machinery. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-4/
- **The Gospel Coalition:** Angels nearest the throne who lead the worship. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/revelation/
- **Carson:** The eyes mean God's throne sees everything. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/revelation-4-en/
- **Barnes:** "Beasts" (KJV) is a poor translation. The word means "living beings." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/4-6.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Takes them as gospel ministers, placed between God and the people. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rev/Rev_004.cfm

---

**v. 7: Lion, calf, man, eagle**

*Traditional reading: the best of all creation*
- **Pulpit:** The four main orders of animal life: wild animals, domestic animals, humans and birds. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/4.htm
- **Constable:** Together they may picture all creation praising God, or God ruling all of it, or both. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-4.html
- **Guzik:** Quotes a rabbinic saying that each of the four is chief of its kind. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-4/
- **Meyer:** Calls this rabbinic view "the correct point of view." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/4-8.htm
- **Wesley** (Methodist): Courage (lion), patient endurance (ox), wisdom and compassion (man), energy (eagle). He reads the eyes as wisdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/revelation-4.html
- **Tribal banners.** Clarke reports a Jewish tradition linking the four to the banners of Judah, Ephraim, Reuben and Dan. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/4-7.html
  - Guzik notes that Numbers 2 doesn't actually assign these symbols. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-4/

*Other views: the four Gospel writers (early church and Catholic)*
- **Victorinus:** Lion = Mark, man = Matthew, calf = Luke, eagle = John. They also picture Christ's preaching, his becoming human, his sacrifice and his ascension. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0712.htm
- **Augustine:** Prefers lion = Matthew (Christ the king), man = Mark, calf = Luke, eagle = John. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1602106.htm
  - The footnote on Bible Hub's copy of this text says Irenaeus and Jerome assigned them differently, and that Jerome's version became standard in medieval art. https://biblehub.com/library/augustine/the_harmony_of_the_gospels/chapter_vi_of_the_four_living.htm
- **Catholic Encyclopedia:** These four became the standard symbols of the Gospel writers in Christian art. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01515b.htm
- **Barclay:** Describes yet another ancient arrangement (lion = John, ox = Luke, man = Matthew, eagle = Mark). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/revelation-4.html
- **Haydock's Catholic Commentary:** Rejects the Gospel-writer reading, partly because John was still alive. It takes the creatures as the four great prophets: Isaiah (royal, lion), Jeremiah (priest, calf), Ezekiel ("son of man"), Daniel (eagle). It notes another Catholic writer who listed thirty interpretations. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/revelation-4.html
- **Coffman:** Sets aside both the Gospel-writer and tribal-banner readings. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/4-6.html

---

**v. 8: Six wings; "Holy, Holy, Holy"**

- **Ligonier:** The threefold "holy" and the six wings suggest the same beings Isaiah saw (Isa. 6). Unlike Isaiah's seraphim, they don't cover their faces. The open eyes may mean the Lord sees everything. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/heavenly-host
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The wings stand for reverence, humility and obedience, and the eyes for constant activity. "Day and night" should probably go with "saying," not with "never stop." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/4.htm
- **Barnes:** The point is that God's works and ways continually bring him praise. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/revelation-4.html
- **Who was and is and is to come:** Precept Austin, quoting Akin, says this phrase looks back to the "I AM" of Exodus 3:14. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-4-commentary
- **Barclay:** Calling God "Almighty" assured readers living under Rome that they were safe. It wasn't a promise of freedom from trouble, but of security in life and death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/revelation-4.html
- **Bible Hub compilation:** Notes that John's creatures each have one face, while Ezekiel's had four faces each. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/4-8.htm

---

**vv. 9–10: The elders fall down and cast their crowns**

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Calls the song a "Eucharistic" (thanksgiving) hymn, giving God the thanks his creation owes him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/4.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** Falling down shows deep reverence. Casting crowns admits that all their grace and glory came from God. The elders worship the same one God as the living creatures, and the true church has only one object of worship. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rev/Rev_004.cfm
- **Guzik:** These are victory crowns, not royal ones. Every reward comes from God, and no one in heaven envies anyone else. Believers should practise laying down their achievements now. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-4/
- **GotQuestions:** These may be the reward crowns promised to faithful believers. It thinks believers will probably follow the elders' example, though Scripture doesn't say so directly. https://www.gotquestions.org/casting-crowns.html
- **Constable:** The crowned rulers willingly place their authority under God's. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-4.html
- **The Gospel Coalition:** It is an act of willing submission. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/revelation/
- **Precept Austin:** "Who lives forever and ever" is God the Father, described in terms very like Jesus in 1:18. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-4-commentary

---

**v. 11: "Worthy are You… for You created all things"**

- **Matthew Henry:** God is worthy as Creator, as sustainer (keeping things in being is a continual creation), and as the purpose of all things. No created thing may be worshipped. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rev/Rev_004.cfm
- **Precept Austin:** He alone is Creator; everything else is a creature. Worshipping anything else is idolatry. The page also notes that the same praise is given to the Lamb in ch. 5, which it takes as evidence of Christ's deity. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-4-commentary
- **The Gospel Coalition:** The same praise goes to the Lamb in 5:12–13. "For" gives the reason God is worthy: he created all things. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/revelation/
- **Barclay:** Humans can rearrange what exists, but only God creates from nothing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/revelation-4.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Mentions a rare variant reading ("they were not, and were created") and says most evidence is against it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/4.htm
- **NET Bible note:** "They existed and were created" seems backwards in time and logic. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=rev&chapter=4&verse=11
- **Coffman:** John's refusal to describe God in human form in v. 3 matches "God is Spirit" in John 4:24. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/revelation-4.html

---

**Gaps worth another search pass**
- **Traditions I couldn't reach:** Lutheran, Pentecostal (besides Enduring Word), Holiness (besides Wesley's notes on v. 7), Orthodox (for example, the link between v. 8 and the "Holy, Holy, Holy" sung in the liturgy) and catholic.com.
- **Popular modern teaching:** I didn't find any prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace material on this chapter.
- **Missing commentary:** Gill on vv. 6–11 and Ellicott on vv. 7–11, because those pages were cut short.
